basic_information.name: RAGAS (Retrieval Augmented Generation Assessment)
basic_information.creator: Exploding Gradients (now operating as VibrantLabs). Founded by Shahul Es and Jithin James. Y Combinator W24 batch. Contact: team@vibrantlabs.com.
basic_information.description: RAGAS is the most widely adopted open-source framework for evaluating Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines and LLM applications. Its core innovation is reference-free evaluation: using LLMs as judges to assess retrieval quality, generation faithfulness, and answer relevancy without requiring human-annotated ground truth data. Published at EACL 2024, RAGAS provides a suite of metrics (faithfulness, context precision/recall, answer relevancy) that have become the de facto standard for RAG evaluation, analogous to how pytest became standard for Python testing. Beyond evaluation, RAGAS generates synthetic test datasets from knowledge bases and supports agentic workflow evaluation with tool-call accuracy metrics. With 800K+ monthly PyPI downloads and 20M+ evaluations processed, it is the dominant open-source RAG evaluation tool, used alongside observability platforms like Langfuse, LangSmith, and Arize Phoenix.
basic_information.release_date: September 2023 (initial arXiv paper 2309.15217); EACL 2024 demo paper (March 2024); v0.4.3 released January 13, 2026 (latest stable release as of Feb 2026)

technical_architecture.architecture_type: Library (open-source Python SDK). Purely a software library that runs locally or in CI/CD pipelines — no server, no managed infrastructure. Evaluations are computed by calling LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.) to judge retrieval and generation quality. Includes CLI tooling for running evaluations from the command line. Async-first architecture using AsyncOpenAI and similar async clients for efficient batch evaluation.
technical_architecture.language: Python (83%), Jupyter Notebook (16.7% — tutorials and examples), minimal other (0.3%)
technical_architecture.embedding_dimensions: Not directly applicable — RAGAS is an evaluation framework, not an embedding model. However, it uses embedding models internally for some metrics (e.g., semantic similarity). Compatible with any embedding model dimension through its adapter system (OpenAI, Cohere, Gemini, Voyage AI, HuggingFace, Ollama).
technical_architecture.indexing_algorithm: Not applicable — RAGAS does not index or store vectors. It evaluates the outputs of RAG systems that use their own indexing. RAGAS operates on the evaluation artifacts: questions, retrieved contexts, generated answers, and optional ground truth.
technical_architecture.scalability: Scales horizontally via batch evaluation and async processing. Can evaluate thousands of samples in parallel using LLM API concurrency. No inherent data limit — evaluation throughput is bounded by the LLM API rate limits used as judges. Processes 5M+ evaluations monthly across the community (as of 2024). Supports batched evaluation runs with progress tracking.
technical_architecture.deployment_options: Local Python installation (pip install ragas), CI/CD pipeline integration, Jupyter notebooks for interactive evaluation, CLI commands for automated evaluation. No managed cloud service with standard pricing tiers — enterprise features available via direct contact with founders. Docker-compatible for containerized evaluation workflows.

rag_specific_capabilities.retrieval_method: RAGAS does not perform retrieval — it evaluates retrieval quality. Metrics assess: context precision (signal-to-noise ratio of retrieved context), context recall (whether all relevant information was retrieved), context entities recall (entity-level recall measurement), noise sensitivity (robustness to irrelevant retrieved content), and response groundedness (whether the answer is grounded in retrieved context). Works with any retrieval method (dense vector, sparse BM25, hybrid, knowledge graph) since it only evaluates the outputs.
rag_specific_capabilities.chunking_strategy_support: Not directly applicable as an evaluation tool. However, RAGAS's synthetic test data generation can create evaluation datasets that stress-test different chunking strategies. The generated test sets include questions of varying complexity (simple, multi-hop, reasoning) that reveal chunking weaknesses. RAGAS can evaluate the impact of different chunking strategies by measuring the same metrics across different pipeline configurations.
rag_specific_capabilities.reranking_support: RAGAS does not perform reranking but can evaluate the impact of reranking on RAG quality. Context precision and context recall metrics directly measure whether reranking improved the relevance ordering of retrieved passages. Teams typically run RAGAS evaluations A/B-testing reranking configurations to measure improvement.
rag_specific_capabilities.multimodal_support: Yes — RAGAS includes multimodal evaluation metrics: Multimodal Faithfulness (evaluates factual consistency of responses generated from multimodal contexts including images and text) and Multimodal Relevance (measures how relevant multimodal responses are to queries). This enables evaluation of vision-RAG pipelines using models like GPT-4o or Claude for multimodal judgment.
rag_specific_capabilities.graph_rag_support: RAGAS can evaluate GraphRAG outputs since it operates on question-context-answer triples regardless of the retrieval source. No specialized GraphRAG metrics yet, but the standard faithfulness and context metrics apply. RAGAS's context entities recall metric partially addresses entity-centric evaluation relevant to knowledge graph retrieval.
rag_specific_capabilities.citation_grounding: RAGAS provides response groundedness as a metric that measures whether generated responses are factually supported by the retrieved context. Faithfulness is the primary grounding metric — it decomposes the answer into claims and checks each claim against the provided context. This is the core value proposition: automated verification that LLM outputs are grounded in retrieved evidence rather than hallucinated.
rag_specific_capabilities.context_window_optimization: Not directly applicable — RAGAS is an evaluation tool, not a RAG pipeline builder. However, RAGAS's metrics help teams optimize context window usage: context precision identifies irrelevant context that wastes window space, and noise sensitivity reveals how much irrelevant context degrades generation quality. RAGAS evaluation results guide teams toward optimal context selection strategies.

performance_and_benchmarks.latency: Evaluation latency depends on the LLM judge being used. A single sample evaluation (one question-context-answer triple) typically takes 2-10 seconds per metric depending on the LLM provider (faster with GPT-4o-mini, slower with Claude Opus). Batch evaluations of 100 samples: 2-15 minutes depending on API concurrency limits. Async processing significantly reduces wall-clock time for large evaluation runs.
performance_and_benchmarks.throughput: Processes millions of evaluations monthly across the community (5M+ reported in 2024, 20M+ cumulative). Individual evaluation throughput depends on LLM API rate limits. With OpenAI's batch API or high-concurrency endpoints, teams report processing 1,000+ evaluation samples per hour. The async-first architecture maximizes throughput within API constraints.
performance_and_benchmarks.accuracy_metrics: RAGAS produces the following metrics (all scored 0-1, higher is better): Faithfulness (factual consistency with context), Context Precision (relevance of retrieved context), Context Recall (completeness of retrieval), Answer Relevancy (response relevance to query), Context Entities Recall (entity-level retrieval completeness), Noise Sensitivity (robustness to irrelevant context), Factual Correctness (against ground truth), Semantic Similarity (embedding-based similarity), plus non-LLM metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, CHRF, Exact Match, String Presence).
performance_and_benchmarks.benchmark_results: RAGAS was validated in the original EACL 2024 paper using the WikiEval dataset, showing strong correlation with human judgments of RAG quality. No standardized benchmark exists for evaluation frameworks themselves — RAGAS is the tool that creates benchmarks for RAG systems, not a system being benchmarked. The paper demonstrated that RAGAS metrics correlate well with human assessments across multiple datasets (NQ, HotpotQA). DeepEval and other frameworks have implemented RAGAS-compatible metrics, confirming its influence as a standard. [uncertain]

integration_and_ecosystem.framework_compatibility: Integrates with all major RAG orchestration frameworks: LangChain (native integration with LCEL chains), LlamaIndex (evaluate LlamaIndex query engines and agents), Haystack (deepset integration for pipeline evaluation), DSPy (can evaluate DSPy-optimized programs). Also integrates with AWS tools: Amazon Bedrock Agents evaluation using RAGAS with LLM-as-a-judge. Framework-agnostic by design — only requires question, contexts, answer, and optional ground truth as inputs, so it works with any RAG implementation regardless of framework.
integration_and_ecosystem.model_compatibility: Supports all major LLM providers as evaluation judges via its adapter system: OpenAI (GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini), Anthropic (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 family), Google (Gemini 2.0 Flash, Gemini 1.5), Mistral (mistral-large). Extended via LiteLLM adapter to 100+ providers including Ollama, vLLM, Groq, AWS Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, DeepSeek, and all HuggingFace-hosted models. The llm_factory function auto-detects providers. Users can choose cheaper/faster models (GPT-4o-mini) for evaluation to reduce costs.
integration_and_ecosystem.mcp_integration_status: No MCP (Model Context Protocol) server found for RAGAS as of February 2026. RAGAS is primarily an evaluation library rather than a tool that would typically expose an MCP interface. However, RAGAS could potentially be wrapped in an MCP server for agent-driven evaluation workflows. [uncertain]
integration_and_ecosystem.data_source_connectors: RAGAS does not connect to data sources directly — it operates on evaluation datasets (question-context-answer triples). However, its synthetic test data generator accepts documents from any source (LangChain Document objects, plain text, or PDFs) to generate evaluation datasets. The evaluation workflow integrates with data stored in Langfuse, LangSmith, or any observability platform that captures RAG traces.
integration_and_ecosystem.observability_integration: Deep integration with major observability platforms: Langfuse (run RAGAS evaluations on production traces, reference-free evaluation on logged RAG interactions), LangSmith (evaluate LangChain traces with RAGAS metrics), Arize Phoenix (integrated evaluation dashboard). Also integrates with Braintrust, Confident AI's DeepEval (which implements RAGAS metrics natively), and general tracing platforms. RAGAS results can be exported to pandas DataFrames, JSON, or logged directly to observability platforms.

pricing_and_cost.pricing_model: Fully open-source under Apache 2.0 — no licensing fees. The primary cost is the LLM API usage for running evaluations (RAGAS uses LLMs as judges). Enterprise features and collaborations available via direct contact with founders (no public pricing tiers). The company behind RAGAS (VibrantLabs/Exploding Gradients) monetizes through enterprise services rather than the open-source framework itself.
pricing_and_cost.free_tier: The entire RAGAS open-source framework is free with no usage limits. Unlimited evaluations, all metrics included, full synthetic test data generation. The only cost is the underlying LLM API calls (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.) that RAGAS uses as judges.
pricing_and_cost.cost_at_scale: RAGAS itself is free at any scale. LLM API costs for evaluation: approximately $0.03-0.15 per evaluation sample using GPT-4o-mini (cheapest recommended judge), $0.10-0.50 per sample with GPT-4o, $0.30-1.00 per sample with Claude Opus. For 1,000 evaluation samples: ~$30-150 with GPT-4o-mini. For 10,000 samples: ~$300-1,500. Using cheaper models or open-source LLMs (via Ollama/vLLM) can reduce costs to near-zero for the judge component. RAGAS provides built-in cost tracking to monitor token usage.
pricing_and_cost.total_cost_of_ownership: Framework cost: $0 (Apache 2.0). LLM judge costs: $30-1,500 per 10K evaluation samples depending on model choice. Compute infrastructure: minimal — RAGAS runs on any machine with Python. CI/CD integration: no additional cost. Main TCO considerations: (1) LLM API costs for evaluation judges, (2) engineering time to set up evaluation pipelines and interpret results, (3) optional observability platform costs (Langfuse free tier available, LangSmith $0-39/month). Total monthly TCO for a startup: $50-500 depending on evaluation frequency and model choice. Can be reduced significantly using open-source judge models.

adoption_and_market.market_position: Leader in open-source RAG evaluation. RAGAS is the most popular open-source RAG evaluation framework and the de facto standard for RAG metrics. Positioned similarly to how pytest became standard for Python testing. Academic pedigree (EACL 2024 paper) provides credibility. However, for enterprise-scale production monitoring with dedicated support, Galileo AI and Confident AI's DeepEval are positioned as more enterprise-ready alternatives. RAGAS dominates the open-source niche while enterprise platforms compete for paid deployments.
adoption_and_market.notable_customers: Specific enterprise customer names are not publicly disclosed. However, RAGAS is widely adopted across the ecosystem: AWS uses RAGAS in official blog posts and documentation for evaluating Amazon Bedrock Agents. Redis, Langfuse, Vectara, Haystack (deepset), and Mistral AI all feature RAGAS in their official documentation and cookbooks. Used by research teams, enterprises building RAG applications, and integrated into MLOps pipelines. The framework processes 5M+ evaluations monthly (2024 data), suggesting thousands of organizations use it. [uncertain]
adoption_and_market.community_size: GitHub: ~12,600 stars, ~1,200 forks, 273 contributors, 263 open issues (as of Feb 2026). PyPI: ~830,000 monthly downloads (pypistats.org). Total evaluations run: 20M+ cumulative. Active Discord community for support and discussion (#questions channel). 5M+ evaluations processed monthly (2024 data). Separate ragas_experimental repository for cutting-edge features.
adoption_and_market.funding_and_valuation: Exploding Gradients (company behind RAGAS) completed a pre-seed funding round (exact amount not publicly disclosed). The company was part of Y Combinator Winter 2024 batch. Subsequently rebranded/reorganized under VibrantLabs. Specific valuation not publicly available. Crunchbase lists the company under 'Exploding Gradients' with minimal disclosed financial details. [uncertain]
adoption_and_market.competitive_landscape: Primary competitors: DeepEval by Confident AI (most direct competitor — open-source, implements RAGAS-compatible metrics, adds agentic evaluation, positioned as 'Pytest for LLMs' with better debugging/explainability), Galileo AI (enterprise-focused, proprietary metrics, highest enterprise adoption, production monitoring), TruLens (open-source evaluation with feedback functions), Braintrust (evaluation platform with built-in RAG metrics), Maxim AI (enterprise evaluation and observability). RAGAS differentiators: academic validation (EACL paper), reference-free evaluation innovation, largest open-source community, broadest framework integration, synthetic test data generation. Weakness vs competitors: metrics are not self-explaining (harder to debug than DeepEval), no built-in dashboard (relies on Langfuse/LangSmith), less enterprise support infrastructure than Galileo.

entrepreneurial_relevance.startup_applicability: Essential for any startup building RAG-powered products. Best fit: teams of 1-50 engineers who need systematic RAG quality measurement without building custom evaluation infrastructure. Budget-friendly: completely free, only LLM API costs. Use case fit: internal knowledge assistants, customer support bots, legal/medical RAG applications, document QA systems — any application where retrieval accuracy and answer faithfulness matter for user trust. Particularly valuable for: regulated industries (healthcare, finance, legal) where hallucination detection is critical, and startups preparing for enterprise sales where RAG quality metrics are a differentiator. Not ideal for: teams that only need basic chatbots without retrieval, or organizations requiring turnkey enterprise monitoring dashboards (consider Galileo or DeepEval for that).
entrepreneurial_relevance.build_vs_buy_guidance: Use RAGAS (free) for: evaluation metrics, synthetic test data generation, CI/CD evaluation pipelines, comparing RAG configurations. Complement with an observability platform when: you need production monitoring dashboards (Langfuse free tier is the natural pairing), trace visualization, or team collaboration on evaluation results. Consider DeepEval when: you need better metric explainability and debugging or Pytest-style test integration. Consider Galileo when: you need enterprise-grade SLA, dedicated support, and auto-adaptive metrics. Self-host open-source RAGAS + Langfuse for maximum control and minimal cost. The most common production pattern is: RAGAS for metrics + Langfuse/LangSmith for observability + custom evaluation scripts for domain-specific checks.
entrepreneurial_relevance.time_to_production: First evaluation run: 30 minutes (pip install, write 10-line script with sample data). Basic evaluation pipeline: 1-2 days (integrate with your RAG system, run on real data, interpret results). CI/CD evaluation pipeline: 1-2 weeks (automated evaluation on every code change, baseline tracking, regression detection). Synthetic test data generation: 1-2 days to generate initial dataset from your knowledge base. Full production evaluation setup with observability: 2-4 weeks (RAGAS + Langfuse/LangSmith + custom metrics + dashboards + alerting).
key_lessons: Start evaluating from day one — even a simple RAGAS evaluation loop with 50 test questions reveals more about your RAG pipeline than weeks of manual 'vibe checks'. The initial investment is minimal (30 minutes setup) but the insight is transformational.

Choose your LLM judge strategically: GPT-4o-mini offers the best cost-accuracy tradeoff for evaluation. Using the same model for both generation and evaluation can introduce bias — consider using a different model family as judge (e.g., Claude to judge GPT-4 outputs).

Faithfulness is the single most important metric for production RAG — it directly measures hallucination. If you track only one metric, track faithfulness. Context precision is the second priority as it reveals whether your retrieval is returning noise.

Synthetic test data generation is RAGAS's underrated superpower — it creates diverse evaluation datasets (simple, multi-hop, reasoning questions) from your knowledge base automatically, solving the 'we have no test data' problem that blocks most evaluation efforts.

Combine RAGAS with an observability platform (Langfuse is the most natural free pairing) from the start. RAGAS provides the metrics; the observability platform provides the dashboard, trace inspection, and historical tracking needed to actually improve your pipeline over time.
entrepreneurial_relevance.no_code_interface: No — RAGAS is a Python library requiring code to use. There is a CLI interface (ragas-cli) for running evaluations from the command line, which lowers the barrier slightly, but it is not a no-code/visual tool. However, RAGAS metrics are accessible through no-code observability platforms like Langfuse (which provides a UI for viewing RAGAS evaluation results) and through DeepEval's dashboard.
entrepreneurial_relevance.session_mapping: Session 2 (Prompt engineering — evaluating prompt quality with answer relevancy metrics), Session 3 (Framing AI projects — RAGAS as part of the evaluation strategy in CRISP-DM methodology, Build vs Buy for evaluation infrastructure), Session 5 (Ethics & governance — faithfulness metrics as hallucination detection, responsible AI measurement)

confidence.data_quality: High — information sourced from official RAGAS documentation (docs.ragas.io), GitHub repository (explodinggradients/ragas), arXiv paper (2309.15217), EACL 2024 proceedings, PyPI statistics, AWS official blog posts, and multiple independent technical reviews from Braintrust, Cohorte, Getmaxim, and Medium. Metrics and features verified against official documentation v0.4.3.
confidence.cross_reference: GitHub statistics verified via GitHub page (12.6K stars, 1.2K forks, 273 contributors). PyPI downloads confirmed via pypistats.org (~830K monthly). EACL 2024 publication confirmed via ACL Anthology and arXiv. Apache 2.0 license confirmed in GitHub repository. Framework integrations confirmed across Langfuse, LangSmith, AWS, Haystack, and LlamaIndex official documentation. Competitive positioning confirmed across Braintrust, Getmaxim, and AiMultiple independent reviews.
confidence.caveats: RAGAS is evolving rapidly — v0.4.x introduces significant API changes from v0.1.x (the version most blog posts reference). Many online tutorials use outdated v0.1.x APIs. The framework's evaluation quality depends entirely on the LLM judge used — cheaper models may produce less accurate evaluations. RAGAS metrics can show non-determinism: the same evaluation run may produce slightly different scores due to LLM temperature and prompt sensitivity (GitHub Issue #1125 documents this). The 5M+ monthly evaluations claim is from 2024 and is self-reported. YC W24 batch membership was mentioned in multiple sources but specific funding amounts are not disclosed. The company's transition from Exploding Gradients to VibrantLabs is not fully documented publicly.
confidence.security_posture: As an evaluation library, RAGAS has a smaller attack surface than RAG systems themselves. Main security considerations: (1) RAGAS sends evaluation data (questions, contexts, answers) to external LLM APIs — sensitive data in evaluation datasets could be exposed to LLM providers, (2) The framework collects basic usage telemetry by default (opt-out via RAGAS_DO_NOT_TRACK environment variable), (3) When using RAGAS to evaluate production traces, ensure PII is scrubbed before sending to external LLM judges. RAGAS does not have built-in data anonymization. For RAG security more broadly: RAGAS faithfulness metrics help detect hallucination but do not protect against knowledge base poisoning, prompt injection through retrieved content, or adversarial attacks on the RAG pipeline itself.
